gaps: Only the LLC filing path is modelled step by step (articles of organization under § 4A-202). The other filed structures follow a similar acceptance pattern but are not modelled: a corporation becomes a body corporate when the Department accepts its articles for record or at a stated time up to 30 days later (§ 2-102(b)); a limited partnership is formed when its certificate is filed (§ 10-201(b)); a partnership becomes an LLP when its certificate is filed (§ 9A-1001(b)). Their content checks are not modelled.
'Department' is the State Department of Assessments and Taxation (§ 1-406(d) names it; the article's definition section is not printed here).

The LLC articles may specify a later effective time (§ 4A-202(b)); the model ends at acceptance and does not model a delayed effective time. Formation requires only 'substantial compliance' with the title, which the boolean compliance table does not capture.

The trade name certificate (§ 1-406(a)) must disclose the identification number the Department assigned to the business, so for an LLC it can only follow formation; the model places it after the acknowledgment. How a sole proprietor obtains that number is not stated in the printed text. § 1-406 applies to 'any person', so it reaches entities as well as individuals; its filing manner is left to Department regulation (§ 1-406(c)).
The trade name certificate lasts 5 years; renewal within 6 months before the end of each 5-year period (§ 1-406(f)(2)) is not modelled.

§ 1-203 is printed twice, as the version in effect and the version taking effect October 1, 2026 (Chapters 198 and 199 of 2025); the fees used here are the same in both. The later version adds limited worker cooperative associations.
Annual reports ($300 for LLCs, LPs and LLPs, § 1-203(b)(3)(ii)), expedited processing and preclearance fees are cited, not modelled.

Local licensing (for example traders' licenses issued through the clerk of the circuit court under the Business Regulation Article) and county or municipal permits are outside the sections printed and not modelled.

Limited partners lose their shield if they take part in control of the business (§ 10-303, not printed); LLC member liability (§ 4A-301) and professional LLCs are not covered by the printed sections. The exceptions in § 5-102(a)(3) let architects, engineers, real estate licensees and veterinarians use other forms than a professional corporation.
Nonstock status is a state corporate form, not federal tax exemption; 501(c) status is outside the Maryland Code and only affects the processing fee (§ 1-203(b)(10)).
